title: Supply Chain Readiness: 10 Questions That Separate the Prepared From the Panicked
summary: How ready is your supply chain? Use this 10-question supply chain readiness scorecard to uncover gaps in visibility, data accuracy, and retailer compliance.
body_markdown:
In this article, learn about:


-


How to assess supply chain readiness using a 10-question scorecard


-


How to identify operational gaps in order visibility, data accuracy, retailer compliance, and supply chain resilience


-


How to calculate your readiness score, prioritize improvements, and track progress over time


---


A supply chain readiness scorecard helps suppliers evaluate how prepared their operations are to handle everyday demands and changing retailer requirements. By examining order visibility, trading partner compliance, and operational resilience, it can reveal weaknesses before they become costly problems.


These 10 questions will help you find out. For each one, choose **yes, partly, or no** . Pay attention to questions that take longer to answer or require a call to another team. Sometimes, not knowing the answer is just as revealing as the answer itself.


When you're finished, you'll have a score, a clearer picture of your operational gaps, and a place to start improving.


## Can You See What Is Happening Across Your Orders?


Order visibility is the foundation of a reliable supply chain. When teams know what's been ordered, what's shipped, and what's delayed, they have more time to address problems before those problems reach the retailer.


### 1. Where Does Every Open Purchase Order Stand Today?


If a buyer asks about a specific purchase order (PO), can you answer in a few minutes without checking three separate systems?


Strong readiness means your team can quickly access reliable order status information. If the answer depends on who you ask, or which spreadsheet someone updated last, visibility may be your biggest gap.


### 2. How Soon Do You Learn a Shipment Will Be Late?


Hearing about a late shipment from the retailer is a warning sign.


The earlier you know about a potential delay, the more options you have, whether that's rebooking a delivery appointment, adjusting a shipment, or notifying the buyer.


Consider when your team typically learns about delays: before they happen, on the expected delivery date, or after someone complains.


### 3. Do Your Inventory Numbers Match What Your Trading Partners See?


Inventory discrepancies can create problems for both suppliers and retailers. An inaccurate availability figure can lead to orders you can't fulfill, while mismatched shipment and receiving records can make it harder to determine what inventory is available.


Ask who reconciles inventory records across your systems and trading partners, and how often those checks happen.


**Related Reading:**[Purchase Order Visibility: Why Buyers Still Call Logistics To Find Out Where a PO Is](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/purchase-order-visibility-why-buyers-still-call-logistics-to-find-out-where-a-po-is)


## Is Your Data Accurate Enough to Trust?


Even the best processes struggle when the information behind them is wrong. Inaccurate item data, manual corrections, and unexplained deductions can reveal problems that affect everything from fulfillment to profitability.


### 4. Who Owns Item Data, and When Did Anyone Last Check It?


Incorrect case packs, weights, or stock-keeping unit (SKU) identifiers can create problems long after an item is first set up. Those errors may eventually appear as rejected orders, shipping discrepancies, or receiving issues.


Someone should be responsible for keeping item information accurate and current. If nobody owns the data, important updates can easily be missed.


### 5. How Many Orders Need Someone to Fix Them by Hand?


Think about how often employees re-key orders, correct advance ship notices (ASNs), or investigate mismatched information.


Every manual correction takes time and creates another opportunity for error.


You don't need a perfect calculation to get started. Even a rough estimate of the percentage of orders requiring manual intervention can help reveal whether your processes are keeping up with demand.


### 6. Can You Explain Every Deduction From Last Quarter?


Pull up your deductions and chargebacks from the previous quarter. For each one, can you identify what caused it, whether it was valid, and whether your team disputed it?


Unexplained deductions can reveal problems across your operation, from inaccurate item data to shipping errors. Understanding the cause can help prevent repeat deductions and identify revenue worth recovering.


**Related Reading:**[Why the Same Deductions Keep Coming Back (and How To Make Them Stop)](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/why-the-same-deductions-keep-coming-back-and-how-to-make-them-stop)


## Can You Keep Up With Trading Partner Requirements?


Every new retailer brings opportunities for growth, along with its own operational expectations. Readiness means having processes that can accommodate those differences without requiring your team to reinvent the wheel.


### 7. How Do You Find Out When a Retailer Changes Its Requirements?


Retailers update labeling, routing, electronic data interchange (EDI), and documentation requirements. Does your team learn about changes through retailer portals, email notifications, or an unexpected chargeback?


Identify who monitors requirement updates and how quickly those changes reach the people responsible for implementing them.


### 8. How Long Does It Take to Add a New Trading Partner?


Adding a retail channel should create an opportunity for growth. But when onboarding requires months of manual setup, testing, and troubleshooting, that opportunity can become an operational burden.


Look at how long it takes your team to establish a new trading relationship, from receiving the requirements to processing the first successful order.


If onboarding consistently takes longer than expected, your existing processes may not be ready to support the next stage of growth.


### 9. Does Your OTIF Match the Way Retailers Measure It?


Your internal on-time, in-full (OTIF) performance might look great. But does the retailer agree? Retailers can use different delivery windows, fill-rate thresholds, and rules for partial shipments. That means a supplier's internal performance report may tell a different story from the retailer's scorecard.


Compare your measurements against each retailer's actual requirements. A strong internal score doesn't help much if it overlooks the metrics your trading partners use.


## What Happens When Something Goes Wrong?


A reliable supply chain needs to function when plans change, systems fail, or key employees are unavailable.


### 10. If One Key Person Were Out for a Week, What Would Stop?


Think about the spreadsheets, workarounds, partner contacts, and undocumented processes that live with one employee.


Would the rest of your team know what to do? Operational resilience depends on documented processes, shared access to critical information, and employees who can step in when needed. A vacation shouldn't turn into a supply chain emergency.


## How Do You Calculate Your Supply Chain Readiness Score?


Give yourself two points for every **yes** , one point for every **partly** , and zero points for every **no** .


**Answer**


**Points**


Yes


2


Partly


1


No


0


With 10 questions, your maximum possible score is 20 points.


### What Does Your Supply Chain Readiness Score Mean?


**Score**


**Your result**


**What it means**


**17–20**


Scale-Ready Operator


Your fundamentals appear strong. Focus on the remaining gaps before they become bottlenecks.


**10–16**


The Growing Pains Club


You have a foundation, but some processes may be slowing you down or creating unnecessary work.


**0–9**


The Firefighter


Several operational gaps need attention. Start with the problems creating the most frequent or costly disruptions.


These scores are a starting point for internal discussion, not an industry benchmark or formal certification.


Your total score tells part of the story. The next step is identifying where you lost the most points.


### Which Part of Your Supply Chain Needs the Most Attention?


Group your answers into the four categories below.

For each category, divide the points you earned by the maximum available points, then multiply by 100.


For example, if you earned three out of six points in order visibility, your readiness score for that category is 50%.


Comparing percentages helps account for the different numbers of questions in each category.


The category with the lowest percentage is a good place to investigate first. However, a single serious compliance or operational risk may deserve immediate attention, regardless of your overall score.


## How Do You Decide Which Supply Chain Gap to Fix First?


You have your score. Now what?


Resist the temptation to tackle every problem at once. Instead, look at the questions where you answered partly or no and evaluate two things:


-


**Impact:** How often does this problem cost your business time, money, or missed opportunities?


-


**Effort:** How much work would it take to make a meaningful improvement?


Start with a recurring problem that has a measurable impact and a realistic solution.


For example, assigning ownership of item data may be a relatively simple change that prevents repeated errors. Improving order visibility across disconnected systems may require a larger project.


Choose one gap, assign an owner, and establish a measurable target. That could mean reducing manual order corrections, shortening trading partner onboarding time, or improving the accuracy of shipment status updates.


### Retake Your Supply Chain Readiness Scorecard in 90 Days


A scorecard becomes more valuable when you use it to measure progress. Save your initial results and revisit the same 10 questions in approximately 90 days. Compare your scores, review the changes your team made, and look for improvements in the areas you prioritized.


You may discover that fixing one problem improves several others. Better item data, for example, can reduce manual corrections, improve fulfillment accuracy, and help prevent certain deductions.


And if a different category becomes your lowest score? That's useful information, too. Your next priority is already waiting.


## Your Supply Chain Just Told You Where to Start


A supply chain readiness scorecard won't prevent every late shipment or unexpected change to retailer requirements. But it can help you recognize the weaknesses that make those problems harder to manage. Start with the gap that creates the most friction, give someone ownership, and measure what improves.


As your business grows, keeping those weak links in check becomes even more important.
